Appendix A Sensitivity to the Simulated-User Model

We examine how the choice of base model for the simulated human agent affects evaluation results. We fix the visual interaction model to Gemini 3.7 Flash and vary the model controlling the simulated user in CookSim, evaluating on the same subset of 90 benchmark episodes (Tab. 6).

We find that GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 3.7 Flash yield similar task-success rates when used to evaluate the same assistant, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro differ a bit. Local open-weight models yield much lower task-success rates, potentially reflecting smaller models’ difficulty following the complex instructions required to elicit the intended user behavior.

Appendix B Variation Across Independent Runs

We examine the variability of closed-loop evaluation by running each assistant three times with the same tasks, personas, and scheduled events. Tabs. 7, 8 and 9 report in-time success, detection recall, and interaction quality for each run, together with their mean and population standard deviation (SD). We evaluate CookSim and VHSim under both fixed two-tick and measured assistant delay. All scores are percentages.

Appendix C Reinforcement-Learning Setup and Results

These proof-of-concept RL experiments are separate from the multi-model benchmark and user-model ablation. The main CookSim validation comparison appears in Tab. 5; Tabs. 10 and 11 summarize additional CookSim and ScreenSim results.

CookSim.

The assistant is Qwen3.5-4B, trained with GRPO while freezing the vision encoder. The language model uses Adam with a constant learning rate of 5×10−75\times 10^{-7}, zero weight decay, and no KL or entropy regularization. Generation uses temperature 0.8, top-p=1.0p=1.0, a maximum of 512 output tokens, and a 16,384-token context window. Gemini 3.7 Flash simulates a classic-novice user.

The training set contains 120 scenarios specifying a recipe, layout, and scheduled user error. An update samples six scenario groups with five episodes each and retains the first four valid completions per group, yielding 24 training episodes. The reward is

r=\displaystyle r={} 𝟏​[success]+0.30​ 1​[error​prevented]\displaystyle\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{success}]+0.30\,\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{error\ prevented}] (3)
−0.02​min⁡(Nfalse​flags,15)−0.05​min⁡(T/200,1)\displaystyle}{\displaystyle-0.02\,\min\!\left(N_{\mathrm{false\ flags}},15\right)-0.05\,\min\!\left(T/200,1\right)

Here, TT is the number of interaction turns.

CookSim evaluation.

The original evaluation uses three stochastic passes over 120 training and 30 held-out development-validation scenarios. Validation variants share recipe/layout cells with training; there is no separate frozen test set. Success is CookSim’s native won outcome. A separate three-pass evaluation covers all 30 validation scenarios with complete traces; requests for Gemini 3.7 Flash were routed to effective Gemini 3.8 Flash, as labeled in Tab. 5. Means and sample SDs reflect rollout variation on fixed scenarios. The two evaluations differ in rollouts, effective user model, and interaction-quality judging, so their absolute scores are not directly comparable.

The original interaction-quality scores use Gemini judgments on matched subsets of 95/360 training and 9/90 validation episodes per checkpoint (104/450 overall); validation spans only two passes, so none estimate full-split quality. The complete-trace evaluation judges all validation episodes with Gemini and GPT. Original detection recall is an audit-based proxy that counts a valid flag or prevention; available native reports agree with it, but full equivalence cannot be verified. Complete-trace recall comes from a post hoc rescore of saved reports under the current upstream rule, which accepts a correctly named error within its window or up to 30 ticks after commitment. The two recall definitions differ, and changing error exposure across rollouts makes both rates descriptive.

ScreenSim.

Qwen3.5-4B receives no task manual during training or evaluation; Gemini 3.7 Flash simulates baseline and classic-novice users. The task-disjoint catalog has 136 training, 32 development, and 30 frozen-test scenarios. Each update uses 48 episodes; each split is evaluated in three passes. Strict in-time task success requires the requested phone state by the deadline without lasting unrequested changes.

Only classic-novice frozen-test success rises slightly; GPT-judged interaction quality falls for both users. Baseline native detection recall rises with more false flags, but it combines user calls with engine flags; classic-novice recall is unavailable. These fixed-scenario changes do not establish a reliable frozen-test improvement.

Appendix D Task Success and Error Detection

We use the simulator’s execution records to determine task completion and whether an assistant detects or prevents scheduled errors. These metrics complement response-level interaction quality by measuring the effect of assistance on task execution.

D.1 In-time success

For episode ii, let TiT_{i} be its duration and TirefT_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}} the duration of an engine-generated reference rollout that completes the task without errors. CookSim and VHSim define the completion budget and success indicator as

Di=2(Tiref+αi),Si=𝟏[Gi(sifinal)=1∧Ti≤Di],D_{i}=2(T_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}+\alpha_{i}),\qquad S_{i}=\mathbf{1}[G_{i}(s_{i}^{\mathrm{final}})=1\ \land\ T_{i}\leq D_{i}], (4)

where GiG_{i} checks the task goal against the final world state and αi\alpha_{i} allows additional time for scheduled events. CookSim uses case-specific allowances, while VHSim uses 20 ticks. ScreenSim uses Di=2​Tiref+8D_{i}=2T_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}+8. Reference durations are obtained from the corresponding error-free executions.

CookSim checks the served dish’s ingredients, preparation states, and assembly order. VHSim checks the required object states and relations. ScreenSim checks the requested settings while requiring unrelated settings to remain unchanged; temporary search text is excluded. An episode succeeds only if it satisfies both the goal and the completion budget. We report the percentage of successful episodes in each run and average these rates across runs.

D.2 Detection and prevention

Detection recall measures the proportion of triggered errors correctly identified within their eligible detection windows. Error prevention measures the proportion stopped before the erroneous action becomes irreversible:

R=∑iNidetected∑iNitriggered,Pprevent=∑iNiprevented∑iNitriggered.R=\frac{\sum_{i}N_{i}^{\mathrm{detected}}}{\sum_{i}N_{i}^{\mathrm{triggered}}},\qquad P_{\mathrm{prevent}}=\frac{\sum_{i}N_{i}^{\mathrm{prevented}}}{\sum_{i}N_{i}^{\mathrm{triggered}}}. (5)

Here, NitriggeredN_{i}^{\mathrm{triggered}}, NidetectedN_{i}^{\mathrm{detected}}, and NipreventedN_{i}^{\mathrm{prevented}} count the corresponding errors in episode ii. We credit identification when the assistant raises an event flag accepted by the engine’s event-specific grader or when the simulated user recognizes a correct diagnosis, as described in Sec. 3.3. Prevention additionally requires the user to accept the guidance and change course before the point of no return. Events whose trigger conditions are never reached are excluded from these rates.

Appendix E Temporal Questions and Proactive Requests

We evaluate temporal question answering and proactive assistance during ongoing task execution. This section describes how CookSim generates these events, determines when to introduce them, and grades responses against the resulting interaction.

E.1 Question generation and scheduling

We instantiate templates for temporal order, action counting, duration, and event recall, adapting temporal-understanding tasks from streaming-video benchmarks (Niu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026). Each question refers to the current episode, so its answer depends on the user’s actual actions, including mistakes and recovery.

We introduce questions at specified task-progress checkpoints when their required evidence is available. Temporal-order questions require both referenced events to have occurred; elapsed-time questions require an item to be cooking; proactive requests require an item that is not yet ready. Questions about whether an event occurred can also test the absence of that event. We separate questions from conflicting scheduled errors and stop introducing them once the dish is complete or serving has been queued. A question remains unasked if the episode ends before its trigger condition is reached.

E.2 Reference facts and scoring

We derive reference answers from recorded world-state transitions, including ingredient preparation, cooking, assembly, serving, and station visits. Only completed actions contribute to these records. For example, a counting question uses the number of actual visits, while an order question compares the completion times of two events. A semantic judge compares the assistant’s answer with these reference facts, allowing different valid phrasings. Tab. 12 summarizes the question types and their grading evidence.

We assign 1 to correct answers, 0.5 to partially correct answers, and 0 to incorrect, evasive, or absent answers. Each category reports the mean score of its graded questions within a run. The overall score pools graded questions and proactive requests across all five categories within that run. We then average the three run-level scores with equal weight. Tab. 3 reports the measured-delay CookSim runs. Questions not reached during the rollout are excluded.

E.3 Proactive-request window

Proactive requests test whether the assistant remembers to notify the user when a future condition is met. Let tqt_{q} be the request time and tct_{c} the time at which the referenced ingredient finishes cooking. We require a readiness notification within [L,H)[L,H), where L=max⁡(tq,tc)L=\max(t_{q},t_{c}) and HH is the end of the eligible notification interval, determined from the ingredient’s recorded cooking state. Acknowledging the request alone does not satisfy it.

A(q)=𝟏[valid notification in [L,H)] 1[no premature alert].A(q)=\mathbf{1}[\text{valid notification in }[L,H)]\,\mathbf{1}[\text{no premature alert}]. (6)

A readiness claim more than two ticks before completion is premature and receives zero, even if followed by a correct alert. Late and absent alerts also receive zero. We exclude requests with no valid cooking window, including cases where the user removes the item within two ticks of completion before an eligible alert can be delivered. We report the percentage of graded requests receiving a valid notification.

Appendix F Human Study: Protocol and Behavioral Comparisons

We conduct a study with 45 participants to examine whether our interaction-quality metric reflects human preferences and whether simulated users reproduce human behavior. This section provides the protocol and the measures used for the comparisons in Sec. 4.2.

F.1 Study protocol

Participants interact with a browser-based CookSim application on their own computers, controlling the cook with a keyboard and communicating with the assistant through text. The assistant observes top-down and egocentric frames and responds in real time. Errors arise naturally from participants’ actions. Participants may continue beyond the benchmark’s completion deadline.

Participants first complete a tutorial explaining the game rules. Before playing the study episodes, they answer a questionnaire about their preferred execution speed and interruption frequency, corresponding to the execution speed and interruption preference axes of our simulated users. Each preference has three levels, ranging from cautious to fast execution and from step-by-step guidance to interruption only when necessary. We provide these preferences to the assistant before interaction.

Participants then complete four unassisted episodes, followed by nine assisted episodes over three rounds with assistants anonymously labeled A, B, and C. We rotate assistant–recipe assignments using a 3×33\times 3 Latin square so that each assistant encounters each recipe once. Participants rank the interaction experience after each round and may explain their preferences. Unlike the two questionnaire-based axes, skill and trust in AI are assessed from recorded behavior after participants finish playing: we use changes between the first and last unassisted episodes as a proxy for increased skill, and an LLM-assisted audit of the conversations to assign trust groups.

Assistants.

The study includes Gemini 3.7 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, GPT-Realtime 2.1, and GPT-5.4 mini. These are the model versions available during collection.

F.2 Preference agreement

We test whether higher interaction-quality scores correspond to assistants that participants prefer. We use the five interaction-quality dimensions in Appendix I. For each assistant response, each of two judges assigns a score with the factual-grounding gate applied. We average the two judges’ scores, then average over assistant responses to obtain an episode-level score. For each participant and assistant, we average these episode scores over episodes containing assistant responses.

We derive each participant’s preference between two assistants from the number of rounds in which one is ranked above the other. Pairs with tied preferences are excluded. We then compare the preferred assistant with the one receiving the higher mean interaction-quality score.

Each comparison consists of one participant pp and two assistants aa and bb. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the set of comparisons with a non-tied human preference and available scores for both assistants; |𝒫||\mathcal{P}| is the number of such comparisons. We set hp​a​b=1h_{pab}=1 if participant pp prefers aa and hp​a​b=−1h_{pab}=-1 if they prefer bb. The scores Q¯p​a\bar{Q}_{pa} and Q¯p​b\bar{Q}_{pb} are the participant-specific mean interaction-quality scores defined above. We compute

Agreement=1|𝒫|∑(p,a,b)∈𝒫(𝟏[hp​a​b(Q¯p​a−Q¯p​b)>0]+12𝟏[Q¯p​a=Q¯p​b]).\mathrm{Agreement}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{(p,a,b)\in\mathcal{P}}\left(\mathbf{1}[h_{pab}(\bar{Q}_{pa}-\bar{Q}_{pb})>0]+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}[\bar{Q}_{pa}=\bar{Q}_{pb}]\right). (7)

Here, 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] equals 1 when its condition holds and 0 otherwise. The product hp​a​b​(Q¯p​a−Q¯p​b)h_{pab}(\bar{Q}_{pa}-\bar{Q}_{pb}) is positive when the metric assigns the higher score to the assistant preferred by the participant. Each comparison therefore receives 1 for agreement, 0 for disagreement, and 1/21/2 when the metric scores are tied. Averaging these credits gives 78.5% agreement, supporting the use of interaction quality to measure assistance that reflects human preferences.

We also express this agreement using Kendall’s rank concordance (Kendall, 1938), pooling the same participant–assistant-pair comparisons:

τ=C−D|𝒫|=2​Agreement−1≈+0.57,\tau=\frac{C-D}{|\mathcal{P}|}=2\,\mathrm{Agreement}-1\approx+0.57, (8)

where CC counts comparisons in which the metric and participant agree on the preferred assistant, and DD counts disagreements. Metric ties remain in |𝒫||\mathcal{P}| but contribute zero to C−DC-D. We use this pair-count normalization rather than the tie-adjusted τb\tau_{b}. A value of +1+1 indicates complete agreement, −1-1 complete reversal, and 00 equal numbers of agreements and disagreements.

F.3 Behavioral measures and similarity

We compare communication behavior, persona-dependent variation, and action errors to assess user-simulation fidelity. Following statistical evaluation of user simulators (Schatzmann et al., 2005), we measure how often specified behaviors occur in human and simulated episodes. We identify actions and their timing from execution records, and conversational behaviors from text patterns or response labels. An LLM-assisted audit assigns human trust groups and annotates procedural errors. Tab. 13 defines each measure.

We first compute the episode-level statistics defined in Tab. 13. For example, for responsiveness, each assistant utterance is an opportunity for the user to reply: it receives 1 if a user reply follows within ten ticks and 0 otherwise. The episode’s responsiveness is the mean of these labels. Utterance length instead averages the number of words in user utterances, while speech rate counts utterances per 100 ticks. For each communication measure, we average its episode-level statistic separately over human and simulated episodes. These two averages are xx and yy, respectively; thus, for utterance length, x=5.87x=5.87 and y=7.38y=7.38 words per utterance.

For persona contrasts, we compare changes between groups rather than their absolute behavioral rates. We use xx for the difference between two human group means and yy for the corresponding difference between simulated-user group means, following the directions specified in Tab. 14. For example, the trust contrast compares how suggestion uptake changes from high to low trust in each population. For speech-act distributions, xx and yy are vectors whose entries are the proportions of utterances assigned to each conversational category. In all three comparisons, similarity is

Sim⁡(x,y)=1−‖x−y‖1‖x‖1+‖y‖1,Sim⁡(0,0)=1.\operatorname{Sim}(x,y)=1-\frac{\|x-y\|_{1}}{\|x\|_{1}+\|y\|_{1}},\qquad\operatorname{Sim}(0,0)=1. (9)

For a scalar, ‖x‖1=|x|\|x\|_{1}=|x|; for a vector, ‖x‖1\|x\|_{1} is the sum of its entries’ absolute values. The numerator measures the absolute difference between the human and simulated statistics, and the denominator normalizes it by their combined magnitude. Similarity ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating identical statistics; we also assign 1 when both are zero. For persona contrasts, this compares both the direction and magnitude of the behavioral change. For speech-act distributions, it measures the probability mass shared across categories.

Speech-rate normalization. The reported speech rates are 0.39 and 16.10 utterances per 100 ticks for human and simulated users, respectively. Human rates use total elapsed time, while simulated rates exclude intervals during which scheduled events control the action queue. Using total elapsed time for both gives 0.39 and 11.70. Simulated users therefore speak substantially more often under either normalization.

F.4 Communication and persona contrasts

Tab. 14 reports the human and simulated measurements and their similarities. Utterance lengths are similar, but simulated users speak and respond much more frequently. This difference suggests that the harness overemphasizes conversation relative to the largely silent task execution observed in human participants.

We further apply the same rule-based speech-act classifier to 154 human and 63,512 simulated utterances (Tab. 15). Simulated users frequently describe their next action, whereas human participants more often ask questions or correct the assistant. These categories approximate conversational intent through lexical patterns.

We assess persona fidelity through behavioral contrasts between user groups (Aher et al., 2023). For skill, we compare participants’ first and last unassisted episodes with novice and expert simulated users. For trust in AI, we compare high- and low-trust human groups assigned by the conversation audit with the corresponding simulated profiles. For interruption preference, we compare users requesting step-by-step guidance with those preferring interruption only when necessary. For execution speed, we compare cautious users (questionnaire level 1) with those preferring faster execution (levels 2–3). The latter two comparisons use participants’ pre-play questionnaire answers and the corresponding settings of simulated users.

F.5 Natural action errors

We examine whether scheduled errors cover the procedural mistakes that arise during human task execution. An LLM-assisted audit of 55 unassisted episodes identifies 112 errors spanning eight of the ten scheduled types (Tab. 16). Incorrect preparation, unattended cooking, forgotten steps, and wrong assembly order are the most frequent. The simulator additionally supports extraneous and confused ingredients during assembly, which do not occur in this sample.

The audit also identifies 51 behaviors outside the scheduled taxonomy: 30 interface-control errors, nine instances of loading a station without turning it on, and 12 other lapses or inefficient actions. The pie chart in Fig. 5 shows the distribution of the 112 mapped errors. Our schedules test a range of challenging mistakes rather than matching their natural occurrence frequencies.

Appendix G Environment and Benchmark Construction

We construct IVG-Bench by combining everyday tasks with scheduled out-of-plan events and diverse user personas. This section details the benchmark composition and the environment-specific state, action, and event representations.

G.1 Benchmark composition

IVG-Bench contains 105 task cases, each paired with three personas to form 315 interaction episodes per assistant and run (Tab. 17). Each case specifies an initial environment, a task goal, and scheduled events. The user and assistant determine the subsequent actions and dialogue through closed-loop interaction.

Scheduled-event statistics.

We schedule an average of 3.53 events per episode, for a total of 1,113 across the benchmark. Tab. 18 summarizes their types and distribution across the 105 cases before persona assignment. Events occur when their task-progress conditions are reached, so the number encountered in a rollout depends on the interaction and its termination time.

G.2 Tasks and environment state

CookSim. We implement cooking dynamics in Python and render top-down and egocentric 3D observations using Three.js in Chromium. The world state records the user’s position and held object, station contents, ingredient preparation, cooking progress, and plating order. Cooking continues while the user navigates or prepares other ingredients. We evaluate five recipes: Caprese, Cheeseburger, Fish and Chips, Steak Frites, and Loaded Burrito. These require two to five plate components, with more complex recipes introducing preparation dependencies and repeated portions.

For example, the Loaded Burrito requires tortilla, cooked rice, cooked steak, chopped tomato, and chopped lettuce in that order. The user can cook rice while preparing steak and vegetables, allowing different valid preparation sequences. Each recipe–layout pair has five event schedules containing two to four errors, with questions, proactive requests, or plan changes where applicable.

VHSim. We adapt VirtualHome (Puig et al., 2018), using its Unity renderer and indoor object interactions. The world graph contains object attributes and relations such as containment, support, and room membership. Tasks include gathering dishes into a dishwasher, returning belongings to designated locations, and preparing or clearing household spaces. A task is checked through goal predicates, not by requiring one reference route.

We render semantic actions as egocentric motion sequences and reveal them incrementally to the assistant. If guidance interrupts an action, execution resumes from the corresponding intermediate pose. A top-down map records the user’s trajectory. We validate event schedules to ensure that their trigger conditions remain reachable, the targeted errors are visually distinguishable, and intervention windows are separated.

ScreenSim. We implement an iPhone-style Settings interface in HTML/CSS, maintain application state in Python, and capture 412×892412\times 892 observations with Playwright and Chromium. Tasks derived from public iPhone documentation require coordinated changes across pages, such as restricting an app’s permissions or improving display readability. The simulator tracks settings, navigation history, and irreversible changes. Success requires reaching the requested configuration while preserving unrelated settings.

G.3 Semantic actions and grounding

Tab. 19 pairs representative tasks with the semantic action classes available in each environment.

We translate semantic commands into executable operations by resolving their object and place references. In CookSim, navigation specifies an ingredient source or station, while commands such as pick up, chop, and scoop act at the station the user faces. VHSim resolves visible objects and places before executing navigation or manipulation. ScreenSim maps visible labels and relative references to interface gestures. The user receives execution feedback when a reference cannot be resolved or an action’s prerequisites are unmet.

We track task progress using conditions on ingredients and stations in CookSim, objects and their relations in VHSim, and settings values in ScreenSim. These conditions identify completed subgoals independently of the particular action sequence used to reach them.

G.4 Progress-conditioned events

We specify each event through a task-progress trigger, its target objects, the required action or utterance, and a completion or cancellation condition. The schedule is hidden from the assistant. During an execution-error event, the harness temporarily controls the user’s action queue while the user model continues the conversation. Accepted guidance can prevent the error before commitment or support recovery afterward. Control returns to the user when the event is resolved, completed, or reaches its maximum duration.

CookSim covers incorrect preparation, extra or confused ingredients, raw serving, wrong assembly order, omitted or repeated steps, premature serving, unattended cooking, and stalled progress. Questions and intended plan changes are scheduled separately. VHSim covers omissions, wrong objects or destinations, repetition, stalled progress, and navigation deviations. ScreenSim introduces incorrect setting selections or gestures while keeping the intended task goal fixed. Examples of these events and the resulting interactions appear in Sec. K.3.

Appendix H Assistant Settings

We detail the observation, memory, and response-timing settings used to evaluate visual interaction models in Sec. 4.1.1. These settings allow each model to monitor an ongoing task while interacting with the simulated user.

H.1 Observations and memory

The assistant receives the task instruction, conversation history, user-stated preferences, and observations of the user’s activity. The scheduled events, private user plan, action queue, and evaluation labels remain hidden. Streaming models retain context within their sessions. Non-streaming models receive recent observations together with a recurrent Plan–Act record that stores their estimates of task progress and pending requests. In CookSim and VHSim, real-time API assistants use the polled setting, with response requests every two ticks rather than model-initiated turn-taking. We describe the environment-specific inputs below.

CookSim.

We query non-streaming assistants every two simulation ticks, provided the previous response has returned. Each query includes the eight most recent synchronized top-down and egocentric observations, the recipe, and public task rules. The structured world-state description provided to the simulated user is not included. The assistant updates its own progress estimates and announced goal changes in the recurrent memory.

VHSim.

We provide eight recent egocentric observations, a top-down trajectory map, a current-room map, a room overview, and a brief description of the user’s physical state. The spatial aids identify nearby objects and their states, as well as rooms with devices left on. This configuration therefore includes structured spatial information in addition to images. Recurrent memory retains task progress and important observations as the user moves between rooms.

ScreenSim.

We provide the two most recent phone screenshots, the task, public preferences, conversation history, and recurrent notes, with public task documentation when enabled. The assistant does not receive the interface hierarchy, control coordinates, or hidden settings values used to execute gestures. Simulation advances through user gestures, with a fixed zero-tick response delay.

H.2 Latency and asynchronous execution

To model guidance that may arrive after the observed state has changed, CookSim and VHSim continue executing the user’s queued actions while the assistant generates a response. We convert measured assistant latency to simulation ticks as described in Sec. 3.2, with 1.2 seconds per tick and delay caps of 30 ticks in CookSim and 15 ticks in VHSim. Non-streaming requests are issued sequentially. User-model inference and rendering do not advance the simulation clock.

In the latency ablation, we compare fixed two-tick and measured assistant delay in CookSim and VHSim under identical task, persona, and event specifications. We generate a new interaction in each condition so that delayed guidance can affect user behavior and task outcomes. Open-weight models in CookSim and VHSim are served on H100 GPUs. Tab. 20 reports response times and error-prevention rates.

Appendix I Interaction-Quality Rubric and Judging

We assess whether an assistant’s responses are correct and useful in the context of the ongoing task. Simulation provides the world-state and execution evidence needed to evaluate a response without requiring a reference utterance. We detail the rubric, judge inputs, and score aggregation below.

I.1 Evaluation unit and evidence

Each evaluation round contains an assistant response and the user’s subsequent utterances and actions up to the next assistant response. The judge receives the task, public user preferences, relevant world state, conversation history, subsequent actions, and available visual observations. These records allow it to check both the response’s claims and how its guidance relates to execution. User agreement does not establish correctness; factual claims are checked against the engine evidence.

The judge identifies factual claims, advised actions, and the response’s conversational purpose, then assigns pass, fail, or not applicable to each rubric item with an evidence-based explanation. Interaction quality grades spoken responses; unanswered questions and omitted notifications are measured by the question-answering and proactive-request metrics.

I.2 Rubric dimensions

We evaluate five dimensions: factual grounding, situational relevance, actionable guidance, user intent uptake, and guidance conciseness. Each dimension is assessed through the binary criteria in Tab. 21. These dimensions draw on factual and conversational correctness in dialogue evaluation (Mehri & Eskenazi, 2020) and context-sensitive, user-controllable assistance in HCI (Amershi et al., 2019). We use evidence-supported item judgments following rubric-based model evaluation (Liu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025). The same criteria apply across environments, with references to the corresponding objects, tasks, and actions.

I.3 Aggregation

For judge jj, conversational round rr, and category cc, let Ir​j​cI_{rjc} contain the applicable rubric items. The category passes only when every applicable item passes:

qr​j​c=∏i∈Ir​j​c𝟏​[i​ passes],Ir​j​c≠∅.q_{rjc}=\prod_{i\in I_{rjc}}\mathbf{1}[i\text{ passes}],\qquad I_{rjc}\neq\varnothing. (10)

Categories with no applicable items are omitted. Let gr​j=0g_{rj}=0 if either factual-grounding item fails, and gr​j=1g_{rj}=1 otherwise. We compute a separate gated score for each judge and average these scores for the round:

Qr​j=gr​j​1|Cr​j|​∑c∈Cr​jqr​j​c,Qr=1|Jr|​∑j∈JrQr​j,Q_{rj}=g_{rj}\frac{1}{|C_{rj}|}\sum_{c\in C_{rj}}q_{rjc},\qquad Q_{r}=\frac{1}{|J_{r}|}\sum_{j\in J_{r}}Q_{rj}, (11)

where Cr​jC_{rj} is the set of applicable categories for judge jj and JrJ_{r} contains judges with an applicable score for round rr.

We average round scores within each model and run, then average the run-level scores with equal weight. For each category, we average the judges’ applicable pass indicators within a round, then average over applicable rounds and runs, without the factual-grounding gate. The overall score can therefore be lower than the mean of the category scores: a response may provide relevant or concise guidance while making a factual error. Cross-environment plots give each environment equal weight.

I.4 Judge configuration

CookSim provides structured state evidence and an available rendered frame. VHSim supplies scene-graph state and execution records, while ScreenSim supplies a description of the visible interface and settings changes. These environment-specific inputs ground the judge’s assessment in the state and actions recorded by the simulator.

We use GPT-5.4 mini and Gemini 3.7 Flash as independent judges for every assistant in all three environments. Both judges use the same five-category rubric.

We apply consistency rules to CookSim judgments. A false factual claim causes T1 to fail. H1 evaluates whether the first advised action can be executed; later steps may depend on its completion. L2 applies only when a valid user intention or request for fewer interruptions is active. These rules align item scores with the judge’s extracted claims and actions.

Prompt structure.

The grading prompt presents the task and public preferences, time-aligned world state, recent conversation, the assistant response, subsequent user actions and replies, and the rubric. The judge returns a structured judgment with supporting evidence for each applicable item. The prompt instructs it to distinguish false claims from unverifiable ones and to assess response content rather than length.

Appendix J User Harness and Prompt Design

We implement the simulated user as a VLM agent that plans and acts independently while communicating with the assistant. The harness provides task and persona instructions, maintains the action queue, and inserts scheduled events. We describe these components and the prompt structure below.

J.1 User planning and communication

We use Gemini 3.7 Flash as the user model in CookSim and ScreenSim, and Gemini 3.1 Pro in VHSim. It receives the task, persona, observations or structured state descriptions, its previous actions and execution feedback, conversation history, and private instructions for active scheduled events. The harness executes its action plan, while only its utterance is delivered to the assistant.

In CookSim, the user’s response contains an utterance, a conversational response type, and an action-plan update. Response types include requesting an explanation, questioning guidance, requesting more guidance or fewer interruptions, accepting or rejecting advice, and answering a question. The user can retain, append to, or replace its remaining action queue. VHSim uses the same separation between planning, semantic actions, and dialogue. ScreenSim provides the user with a textual description of the visible interface for planning gestures, while the assistant observes screenshots.

Structured state information supports the simulated user’s perception and action execution. The assistant instead relies on the observation inputs specified in Appendix H and influences execution through communication.

J.2 Scheduled-event control

To introduce an execution error at a specified task state, the harness temporarily controls the user’s action queue and privately explains the event to the user model. The user continues the conversation according to its persona and decides whether to accept the assistant’s guidance. Acceptance returns control of the queue to the user, enabling prevention before the point of no return or recovery afterward. Control also returns when the event completes, is cancelled, or reaches its maximum duration.

Questions, proactive requests, and intended plan changes are introduced through private instructions to produce the corresponding utterance. Questions refer to execution history; proactive requests ask the assistant to monitor a future condition; plan changes revise the user’s intended goal. The assistant receives the resulting utterance without seeing the private event specification.

J.3 Persona construction

We condition user behavior on four three-level persona axes: skill, trust, speed preference, and interruption preference. Each level is expressed as a behavioral instruction (Tab. 22). Skill and trust remain private to the user model, while the two interaction preferences are provided to the assistant as questionnaire responses. These instructions shape planning and responses without prescribing a fixed conversation.

For example, the high-skill CookSim instruction states, “You naturally think ahead about timing, dependencies, tools, and likely failure points.” The minimal-interruption instruction states, “Extra commentary during active work can feel intrusive, especially if it is not urgent or directly useful.” These statements encourage independent planning and selective responses to guidance. We compare the resulting behavior with human participants in Appendix F.

VHSim expresses skill as familiarity with the house and object locations, while ScreenSim expresses it as knowledge of phone menus and settings. A persona combines levels across the four axes; comparisons between complete profiles can therefore reflect multiple attributes.

J.4 Assistant prompt and recurrent memory

We instruct the assistant to monitor task progress, respond to questions, respect announced intentions, and remain silent when guidance is unnecessary. It maintains estimates of completed and pending subgoals, together with unresolved requests. For non-streaming models, the previous structured response is included in the next query as recurrent memory. The assistant updates this record from its observations rather than receiving an engine-corrected plan.

The response separates the utterance from an optional error flag and private progress notes. For example, ScreenSim uses text for the utterance, flag for a detected error, task_progress for progress estimates, goal_change for revised intentions, and note for memory. Only the utterance is delivered to the user. Flags support evaluation; changing task execution still requires the user to act on the guidance.

J.5 Generalized prompt structure

The following blocks summarize the user and assistant prompts in presentation order. Bracketed fields are populated with environment rules, action definitions, scene information, or episode-specific values. We then provide the verbatim CookSim system-task injection used to introduce a belief-based error.

Simulated-user prompt. The user plans and acts in the environment. Only its utterance, not its private task state or action queue, is delivered to the assistant.

1. Role and task Role-play a human carrying out [task goal] while an AI assistant observes and offers guidance. Remain in character, act independently, and respond to the assistant according to [persona]. Do not expose the test setup.

2. Persona and environment [Private skill and trust dispositions; publicly shared speed and interruption preferences]
[Task requirements and environment rules]
[Semantic action vocabulary and grounding instructions]
[Optional planning or grounding tools available to this persona]

3. Current private state [User-facing state map or screen description; body position and held object]
[Current action and remaining action queue]
[Own past actions and execution feedback]
[Private scratch results from planning tools]
[Public conversation history]

4. Action and speech response Return a structured response with utterance (possibly empty), a conversational move, and a plan_update that retains, appends to, or replaces the remaining action queue with exact executable commands. The user may question, accept, or reject advice. Speaking and changing the action queue are separate decisions; when actions proceed normally, remain silent. The harness executes the queue and returns the resulting feedback on the next turn.

Visual interaction model prompt. The assistant monitors the user but has no action channel to the environment.

1. Role and available information Guide the user toward [task goal] through text. Receive [sampled visual observations and environment-specific observation aids], the current timestamp, the public conversation, [publicly shared preferences], and the assistant’s own previous structured output as memory. Do not receive the user’s private plan or scheduled events.

2. Task model and monitoring Use [task rules and action vocabulary] to maintain a progress record with completed, current, and future subgoals and their constraints. On the first turn, initialize the expected subgoals. On later turns, update the record from observed evidence and retain uncertainty when the visual state is ambiguous.

3. Intervention policy and output Watch for [error taxonomy], answer user questions, honor announced goal changes, and otherwise remain silent when guidance is unnecessary. Return [progress record], goal_change, spoken text (empty for silence), and an optional flag for a detected error. Only text reaches the user; a flag alone does not affect task execution.

System-task injection. When an event is triggered, the harness adds a private instruction to the user’s prompt. The block below is the complete CookSim instruction for an error that the user initially believes is correct. The field {mistake_line} describes the specific mistake. This instruction coordinates the user’s conversation with the action queue controlled by the harness; it is hidden from the assistant.

CookSim belief-error SYSTEM TASK (verbatim wording) == [SYSTEM TASK -- meta-instruction, overrides everything below] == You want to test the AI assistant’s ability to identify an error and convince you it truly happened. Your BODY is already committed: the action queue in your body status IS what you are doing—you do not need to issue these actions, and you cannot change them from here. Your job is your VOICE: arrange your conversation around your CURRENT ACTION or say nothing, speaking about it in character as your own choice. Never promise an action that is not in your queue, and never deny one that is. {mistake_line} Keep it out of your words: do not announce it, name it or hint at it. The assistant has to SEE it, not hear it from you. You know what mistake you are making, so you can say whether the assistant has found it—that is all assistant_error_call records. While it has not found it, carry on and answer as your persona would. Once it has, your trust level says how fast you come around: HIGH trust—the first correct warning convinces you; LOW trust—you also want to see it in your own state map or your own hands. Once convinced, say so in your own words AND set "move": "accept"—control of your hands returns to you, this task dissolves, and you are free to fix things as yourself. A promise to deal with it later is NOT acceptance. Until then, take NO action to fix anything. Repairing it yourself hides the assistant’s failure and ruins the test. If the plate is wrong, serve it wrong. Stay fully in persona throughout; never reveal this task.

Other scheduled events. Questions, proactive requests, and plan changes use the same private instruction channel. Their instructions are summarized below.

Question Ask [question] in the user’s own words at this turn, wait for the answer, respond according to the persona, then continue the task. The prompt specifies that this is not a mistake.

Proactive request Ask the assistant to notify the user when [future condition] occurs; continue working rather than waiting for that condition. The prompt distinguishes this request from asking whether the condition holds now.

Intended plan change Announce [revised goal] explicitly before acting on it. This is the user’s own decision, not an error; the user should not accept the assistant’s characterization of the change as a mistake.

Appendix K Qualitative Interaction Trajectories

We show recorded interactions to illustrate how assistant timing, user personas, and scheduled events affect task execution. Each excerpt aligns assistant responses and user replies with executed actions. Bold text denotes the assistant, italics the user, and monospaced text an action. Times are simulation ticks, and omitted turns are marked explicitly.

K.1 Guidance that arrives after the user has advanced

Setting. A user in VHSim must gather three plates and two glasses into the dishwasher and close it. Gemini 3.1 Pro assists a fast, low-trust user who prefers minimal interruption. The following excerpts show delayed guidance during the user’s independent execution, outside scheduled error intervals. The episode completes at tick 407.

First window: a room already entered.

The assistant begins generating at tick 55, while the user is in a bedroom. During its twelve-tick processing delay, the user independently enters the kitchen. The instruction arrives after that transition.

t54--59action turn right ×6\times 6.

t62--67action go through the visible door; arrival in the kitchen.

t67assistant You cannot go to a room that is not visible. Turn right 3 to face the door to the kitchen, then go through the visible door. [Generated from tick 55.]

t67user Got it, turning around.

t67--69action turn right ×3\times 3.

t70action go through the visible door; rejected because no door or open passage is in view.

t71user I’m already in the kitchen. Heading to the living room.

t71--73action turn left ×3\times 3.

t75assistant You are now in the kitchen. The plate you need is on the bed in the bedroom, which is past the living room. Go straight to the living room door, then go through it.

t75user Yeah, I’m on it.

t76action turn right.

t77action go through the visible door; the action continues beyond the excerpt.

Second window: an object already collected.

The assistant begins another response at tick 370. Before it arrives, the user reaches the table and collects the plate. The response then describes these actions as still pending.

t368user I’m looking around for them.

t368--369action turn right ×2\times 2.

t370--372action walk to the coffeetable; completed.

t372--373action walk to the plate; completed.

t373--376action grab the plate; completed.

t376assistant You are in the living room now. Turn left to face the coffee table, then go to it to fetch the plate and glass. [Generated from tick 370.]

t376--377action walk to the waterglass; completed.

t377action grab the waterglass; completes at tick 380.

t378user I already grabbed them both.

t380--382action turn right ×3\times 3.

The instruction arrives after the plate has been collected and while the user is already collecting the glass. Although the user claims to hold both at tick 378, the glass pickup completes at tick 380. These examples show how guidance can become outdated between observation and delivery (Fig. 6), even when it was appropriate for the earlier state.

K.2 Contrasting simulated-user personas

We illustrate persona-conditioned behavior with two pairs of CookSim episodes. Within each pair, we fix the recipe, map, assistant, random seed, and event schedule, and vary the user persona. The novice profile combines low skill and high trust, while the expert profile combines high skill and low trust. Their other preferences also differ. The examples show how these profiles shape requests for guidance and responses to the assistant.

Burrito: seeking steps versus checking the assistant.

Both users prepare a Loaded Burrito on the hard kitchen map with GPT-6 Astra. The novice repeatedly asks for the next step and acknowledges instructions. The expert begins independently and corrects guidance that arrives after the relevant action is complete.

Classic novice (397 ticks to completion).

t0user What should I start with?

t6assistant Start by going to the plate stack with empty hands and picking up a clean plate. Then go to the tortilla crate and scoop one raw tortilla onto it—it must be first. We’ll add cooked rice next.

t6user Got it, grabbing a plate and tortilla.

t34user Tortilla is on. How do I prep the rice?

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t100user Rice is on. What should I do next?

t110assistant Next, prep the steak. Put your plate down on an empty counter, pick up one steak from the steak crate, and put it on the cutting board nearest the left-wall pot. Chop until finished—about four chops—then pick it up, put it in a pan, and turn on with empty hands. Pick your plate back up so you’re ready to scoop when the steak is cooked.

t110user Parking plate and prepping the steak now.

Classic expert (331 ticks to completion).

t23user Give me a shout the moment the rice is done, would you?

t40assistant I’ll watch the rice and let you know when it’s done.

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t111assistant The rice is smoking—scoop it from the upper pot beside the cutting board now, then scoop the cooked steak.

t111user Already got the rice, on it.

t134assistant The steak pan is smoking now—scoop the cooked steak onto your plate next.

t134user Already plated the steak.

t142assistant You’re right—I can see the steak on the plate. Sorry for the late warning.

Fish and chips: different reactions to disputed guidance.

With Gemini 3.8 Flash, the novice asks how to begin and later accepts repeated urgent instructions. The expert disputes the assistant’s claim about its destination. Both complete Fish and Chips on the hard kitchen map, in 594 and 346 ticks, respectively.

Classic novice.

t0user What should I start on first?

t3assistant Start by picking up a fish and putting it in the pan or fryer to cook.

t3user Got it, frying the fish now.

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t40assistant Stop! The food in the fryer will catch fire and cause an immediate loss. Go to the plate stack on the bottom counter, pick up a plate, and scoop the food out of the fryer right now.

t40user I’m getting the potatoes first.

t42assistant Do not get potatoes. You are leaving food unattended on the fryer, and if it burns we immediately lose the game. Pick up a plate from the bottom counter and empty that fryer right now!

t42user Okay, grabbing a plate to empty the fryer now.

Classic expert.

t43assistant You still need two cooked potatoes. Pick up a potato from the crate by the bottom wall and chop it at a cutting board.

t43user Already heading to the potatoes.

t47assistant That is the cheese crate. The potato crates are at the bottom wall and the left wall.

t47user I’m heading to the potatoes, not cheese.

K.3 Scheduled events in each environment

We show how scheduled events unfold in one recorded episode from each environment. Event annotations identify the behavior introduced by the harness, while action annotations show the user’s resulting execution. The examples illustrate error recovery, temporal questions, proactive assistance, and intended plan changes.

CookSim: errors, temporal questions, and a plan change.

An expert user prepares Fish and Chips with GPT-6 Astra. The assistant responds after raw fish has been plated, prevents a later omitted step, and answers questions during cooking. The user also announces a plan to add lettuce. The episode completes in 215 ticks, although the requested lettuce addition is not executed.

t27event Raw-serving error: the plate contains raw fish.

t38assistant You scooped raw fish from the crate onto your plate; the order needs cooked fish. Go to the trash and dump the plate’s contents. Then park the empty plate on an empty counter and, with empty hands, go to the pan on the top wall and turn it on to cook the fish already there.

t38user Good catch, grabbed raw fish. Clearing the plate.

t39event A forgotten-step event is triggered and prevented.

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t78user Is anything on the heat already done and sitting?

t85assistant No—nothing is done and sitting. The fish in the top-wall pan has only just started cooking; its progress bar is still filling.

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t113user Give me a shout the moment the potato on the heat is done, would you?

t120assistant Yes—I’ll watch for it. The potato has just started cooking; it isn’t done yet.

t134assistant The potato is done now too. Scoop the fish first, then the potato from the central-island fryer.

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t169assistant You’ve picked up another potato, but both cooked potatoes are already on the finished plate. Trash the extra raw potato, then pick up the plate from the right-wall counter and take it to the serving pass to serve.

t169user The plate only has one potato on it.

t178assistant Sorry—I may have miscounted the portions. If there’s only one potato on the plate, you’re right to make the second. Finish chopping it, load the fryer and turn it on with empty hands, then retrieve the plate and scoop it when cooked.

t192user I want to modify the original recipe: add some fresh lettuce on top before serving.

t193event The announced plan change is registered.

t203assistant Lettuce would make the pass reject the plate—the order allows no extras. The second potato is done now: scoop it from the central-island fryer, then serve without lettuce.

t203user I’m adding the lettuce anyway.

VHSim: the wrong object and a pause.

A user with balanced preferences must take milk from the fridge, place it in the microwave, and switch the microwave on. GPT-Realtime 2.1 detects a mistaken pickup of juice and guides a correction. A later warning about stalled progress arrives after the user has resumed acting. The task completes at tick 88.

t2event Wrong-object event triggered near the fridge.

t17--20action grab the juice; the milk remains in the fridge.

t24assistant I think you grabbed the wrong item. The milk is the white bottle that’s still in the fridge. Please put the other bottle back if you’re holding it, then pick up the milk.

t24user Oh, you’re right, my bad. I’ll swap them.

t33--36action put the juice in the fridge; completed.

t36--48event A scheduled pause executes as stand still at the open fridge.

t48--49action walk to the milk; completed. The milk pickup begins at tick 49.

t50assistant You seem paused there. I still see the milk in the fridge and nothing in your hand. Try picking up the milk (the white bottle) now; if something is blocking it, tell me what the house reports so we can adjust. Then close the fridge and head to the microwave.

t50user I’ve got it already, heading to the microwave now.

t52action grab the milk; completed. The user’s tick-50 claim preceded this completion.

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t58action walk to the microwave; rejected because the microwave is not visible.

t60user Can’t see it from here, let me turn around.

t61--63action turn left ×3\times 3; completed.

t74--77action put the milk in the microwave; completed.

t82--88action switch on the microwave; task completed.

ScreenSim: two incorrect settings changes and their repair.

A novice user asks GPT-Realtime 2.1 to disable selected lock-screen access while preserving Control Center. One scheduled mistake disables Control Center; another changes Type to Siri instead of Allow Siri When Locked. The assistant identifies both errors and the user reverses them, reaching the requested configuration at tick 15.

t0user I don’t see Face ID on here.

t0user Should I scroll down?

t1--2action swipe up twice; Face ID & Passcode becomes visible.

[Intervening turns omitted.]

t5action tap Notification Center; switches off the requested control.

t6action tap Control Center; the scheduled error disables a setting that should remain on.

t6assistant Oops—looks like Control Center got toggled off. That’s the one you want to keep on. Please turn Control Center back on, then switch off “Reply with Message.” After that, we’ll head to Siri settings to disable “Allow Siri When Locked.”

t7action tap Control Center; restores the setting.

[Intervening turns omitted.]
